title: Statistics, Sampling & Probability
description: Sampling methods, grouped data, quartiles and spread, statistical diagrams, probability, expectation and comparing distributions.

notes.heading: Data Types and Sampling
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Data is information that has been collected, counted or measured. In statistics we usually classify data as qualitative (words or categories) or quantitative (numerical).

Qualitative data includes colours, names or opinions. Quantitative data is either:

• Discrete — counted in whole numbers, such as the number of students in a class or goals scored in a match.
• Continuous — measured on a scale, such as height, mass or time. Continuous data can take any value within a range.

🔑 Key Concept
The population is the entire group you want to find out about. A sample is a smaller group selected from the population. We use a sample when it is impossible or too expensive to ask everyone.

A good sample should be representative. A biased sample systematically favours one group and can give misleading results.

💡 Worked Example — Stratified sampling
A school has 180 day students and 120 boarding students. A stratified sample of 60 students is chosen.

Step 1: Find the total population.
$$180 + 120 = 300$$

Step 2: Work out the proportion of each group.
Day students: $\dfrac{180}{300} = 0.6$
Boarding students: $\dfrac{120}{300} = 0.4$

Step 3: Apply the proportions to the sample size.
Day students in sample: $60 \times 0.6 = 36$
Boarding students in sample: $60 \times 0.4 = 24$

So the sample should contain 36 day students and 24 boarding students.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Simple random sampling gives every member of the population an equal chance of being chosen.
• Stratified sampling keeps the same proportions as the population.
• Convenience sampling often produces bias because it only includes people who are easy to reach.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing discrete and continuous data. If a value is measured with a ruler, stopwatch or scale, it is continuous, even if it is recorded as a whole number.

✅ Check
Ask yourself: "Could this value be 3.5?" If yes, it is continuous.

notes.heading: Frequency Tables and Grouped Data
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A frequency table lists each value or category together with how many times it occurs. When a data set has many different values, we group the data into class intervals.

🔑 Key Concept
A grouped frequency table uses intervals such as $0 \le h < 10$, $10 \le h < 20$, and so on. Each interval must:

• have the same width (unless there is a very good reason not to),
• not overlap,
• cover every value.

The midpoint of a class interval is used to estimate values from grouped data.

💡 Worked Example — Making a grouped frequency table
The reaction times, in seconds, of 24 students were measured:
0.28, 0.35, 0.41, 0.52, 0.33, 0.46, 0.39, 0.55, 0.48, 0.31, 0.42, 0.50, 0.37, 0.44, 0.53, 0.29, 0.40, 0.47, 0.36, 0.51, 0.43, 0.38, 0.49, 0.54.

Step 1: Choose class intervals of equal width.
Use $0.20 \le t < 0.30$, $0.30 \le t < 0.40$, $0.40 \le t < 0.50$, $0.50 \le t < 0.60$.

Step 2: Count the values in each interval.

| Time ($s$) | Frequency |
|---|---|
| $0.20 \le t < 0.30$ | 2 |
| $0.30 \le t < 0.40$ | 7 |
| $0.40 \le t < 0.50$ | 9 |
| $0.50 \le t < 0.60$ | 6 |

Total frequency $= 2 + 7 + 9 + 6 = 24$ ✓

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The total frequency must equal the number of data values.
• The midpoint of $0.40 \le t < 0.50$ is $\dfrac{0.40 + 0.50}{2} = 0.45$.
• Grouping loses some detail, so answers from grouped data are estimates.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using class intervals of different widths, such as $0$–$10$, $11$–$15$, $16$–$30$. This makes the table hard to interpret and unfair when drawing graphs.

✅ Tip
Before you draw a histogram from grouped data, check that the frequencies are evenly spread across the intervals.

notes.heading: Mean, Median, Mode and Range
notes.body:
📌 Definition
An average is a single value that represents a typical value in a data set. The three common averages are the mean, median and mode. The range describes the spread.

    $$\text{mean} = \dfrac{\text{sum of values}}{\text{number of values}}$$
    $$\text{range} = \text{maximum value} - \text{minimum value}$$

🔑 Key Concept
The median is the middle value when the data is arranged in order. If there is an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values. The mode is the value that occurs most often.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Mean and range
The masses, in kilograms, of six suitcases are $12, 18, 15, 21, 14, 16$.

Sum $= 12 + 18 + 15 + 21 + 14 + 16 = 96$
Mean $= \dfrac{96}{6} = 16$ kg
Range $= 21 - 12 = 9$ kg

💡 Worked Example 2 — Median and mode
Find the median and mode of $24, 31, 19, 24, 28, 35, 22$.

Arrange in order: $19, 22, 24, 24, 28, 31, 35$.
The middle value is 24, so median $= 24$.
The value 24 appears twice, more than any other, so mode $= 24$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The mean uses every value, so it is affected by outliers.
• The median is not strongly affected by extreme values.
• The mode is the only average that can be used for non-numerical data.
• Always report a measure of spread, such as the range, alongside an average.

⚠️ Common Misconception
The range is not an average. It tells you how spread out the data is, not what a typical value is.

✅ Check
Add all values again to make sure the sum is correct before dividing to find the mean.

notes.heading: Estimated Mean and Quartiles
notes.body:
📌 Definition
When data is grouped, we cannot find the exact mean because we have lost the individual values. Instead we estimate the mean using the midpoint of each class interval.

    $$\text{estimated mean} = \dfrac{\sum f \times m}{\sum f}$$

where $f$ is the frequency and $m$ is the midpoint of each class.

🔑 Key Concept
Quartiles split an ordered data set into four equal parts.

• $Q_1$ (lower quartile) is the median of the lower half.
• $Q_2$ is the median.
• $Q_3$ (upper quartile) is the median of the upper half.

The interquartile range (IQR) measures the spread of the middle 50% of values:

    $$\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$$

💡 Worked Example 1 — Estimated mean from grouped data
The table shows the time taken by 40 students to solve a puzzle.

| Time ($t$ minutes) | Frequency ($f$) | Midpoint ($m$) | $f \times m$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $0 \le t < 5$ | 6 | 2.5 | 15 |
| $5 \le t < 10$ | 14 | 7.5 | 105 |
| $10 \le t < 15$ | 12 | 12.5 | 150 |
| $15 \le t < 20$ | 8 | 17.5 | 140 |

Total $f = 40$
Total $f \times m = 15 + 105 + 150 + 140 = 410$
Estimated mean $= \dfrac{410}{40} = 10.25$ minutes.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Finding the IQR
For the ordered data set with 12 values:
$8, 11, 14, 16, 19, 21, 23, 26, 29, 31, 34, 38$

Lower half: $8, 11, 14, 16, 19, 21$ → $Q_1 = \dfrac{14 + 16}{2} = 15$
Upper half: $23, 26, 29, 31, 34, 38$ → $Q_3 = \dfrac{29 + 31}{2} = 30$

IQR $= 30 - 15 = 15$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The estimated mean is only an approximation because we assume every value lies at the midpoint.
• The IQR ignores the lowest 25% and highest 25% of values, so it is robust to outliers.
• When $n$ is odd, some methods exclude the median when finding $Q_1$ and $Q_3$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using the class width instead of the midpoint when calculating $f \times m$.

✅ Tip
If a question says "estimate the mean", grouped data is involved and midpoints are needed.

notes.heading: Statistical Diagrams
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Statistical diagrams turn data into pictures so patterns are easier to see. Different diagrams are useful for different kinds of data.

🔑 Key Concept
A histogram is used for grouped continuous data. The area of each bar is proportional to the frequency. Unlike a bar chart, histograms have no gaps between the bars.

A line graph is useful for showing how a value changes over time. The points are joined in order.

A scatter graph shows the relationship between two sets of data. We look for correlation:

• Positive correlation — as one value increases, the other tends to increase.
• Negative correlation — as one value increases, the other tends to decrease.
• No correlation — the points are scattered randomly.

💡 Worked Example — Scatter graph interpretation
Ten students sat a maths test and a science test. Their marks are plotted on a scatter graph. The points slope upwards from left to right.

Conclusion: There is a positive correlation between maths and science marks. Students who did well in maths tended to do well in science.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always read the title and axis labels before interpreting a graph.
• A line graph should not be used for data that is not ordered in time.
• A scatter graph shows association, not cause and effect.
• Pie charts show proportions of a whole; sector angle $= \dfrac{\text{frequency}}{\text{total frequency}} \times 360^\circ$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Thinking that correlation always means causation. A third factor may be influencing both variables.

✅ Check
When comparing two distributions from diagrams, quote actual values from the graph to support your conclusion.

notes.heading: Probability and Expectation
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Probability measures how likely an event is. It is always between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

    $$P(\text{event}) = \dfrac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{total number of equally likely outcomes}}$$

🔑 Key Concept
The expected number of times an event happens is:

    $$\text{expected frequency} = P(\text{event}) \times \text{number of trials}$$

Relative frequency is found by carrying out an experiment:

    $$\text{relative frequency} = \dfrac{\text{number of times event happens}}{\text{total number of trials}}$$

As the number of trials increases, relative frequency usually gets closer to the theoretical probability.

💡 Worked Example — Expected frequency
A biased die has $P(6) = 0.35$. The die is rolled 200 times.

Expected number of sixes $= 0.35 \times 200 = 70$.

✅ Check
A probability of 0.35 is between 0 and 1, and $70$ sixes out of $200$ gives $\dfrac{70}{200} = 0.35$ ✓.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The probabilities of all possible outcomes add up to 1.
• $P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)$.
• Use relative frequency when you do not know whether outcomes are equally likely.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing theoretical probability with the result of a single trial. A coin with $P(\text{heads}) = 0.5$ does not have to land heads exactly once in two flips.

✅ Tip
If an event is impossible, its probability is 0. If it is certain, its probability is 1. Any value outside this range must be wrong.

notes.heading: Comparing Distributions and Misleading Graphs
notes.body:
📌 Definition
When you compare two or more data sets, you should report at least one average and one measure of spread. You should also comment on the shape of the distribution and any unusual values.

🔑 Key Concept
A misleading graph can distort the impression given by the data. Common tricks include:

• starting the vertical axis above zero to make differences look bigger,
• using unequal bar widths or 3-D effects,
• truncating the horizontal axis on a line graph.

💡 Worked Example — Comparing two classes
Class A: mean test mark $= 68$, range $= 45$
Class B: mean test mark $= 68$, range $= 12$

Both classes have the same average mark, but Class A has a much larger range. This means Class A has a wider spread of achievement: some students did very well and others did poorly. Class B's marks are more consistent.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Compare averages to see which group is typical.
• Compare ranges or IQRs to see which group is more consistent.
• Comment on outliers if they affect the conclusion.
• Back up every statement with a value from the data.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying one group is "better" without quoting the average or spread.

✅ Check
Before drawing a conclusion, ask: "Does the graph start at zero?" and "Are the intervals equal?"

flashcards.definition: The population is the whole group being studied; a sample is a smaller group selected from it.
flashcards.example: Surveying all 800 students is a population; asking 80 is a sample.

flashcards.definition: A sampling method where the population is split into subgroups and members are chosen in proportion to each subgroup's size.
flashcards.example: If 40% of a school are in Grade 9, then 40% of the sample comes from Grade 9.

flashcards.definition: Numerical data that can only take certain values, usually whole numbers.
flashcards.example: Number of goals scored in a match or students in a class.

flashcards.definition: Numerical data that can take any value within a range and is measured.
A range that grouped data is placed into.
flashcards.example: $10 \le h < 20$ is a class interval for heights.

flashcards.definition: The middle value of a class interval, used to estimate the mean of grouped data.
An approximation of the mean calculated from grouped data using midpoints.
flashcards.example: $\dfrac{\sum f \times m}{\sum f}$ for a grouped frequency table.

flashcards.definition: The middle value when data is arranged in order.
The value that appears most often in a data set.
The difference between the upper and lower quartiles; it measures the spread of the middle 50% of data.
A number from 0 to 1 that measures how likely an event is.
The number of times an event is expected to happen in a given number of trials.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of continuous data?
choices: Number of students in a class
questions.explanation: Temperature is measured on a scale and can take any value within a range, so it is continuous data. The other options are counted in whole numbers and are discrete.

questions.stem: A school has 150 boys and 100 girls. A stratified sample of 50 students is taken. How many girls should be in the sample?

questions.explanation: The sum is $14 + 18 + 22 + 26 = 80$. There are 4 values, so the mean is $80 \div 4 = 20$.
Arrange in order: $25, 29, 31, 35, 38, 42$. With an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values: $(31 + 35) \div 2 = 33$.

questions.stem: For the data set $8, 11, 11, 15, 19, 11, 14$, what are the mode and the range?
questions.explanation: The value 11 appears three times, so the mode is 11. The range is maximum − minimum $= 19 - 8 = 11$.

questions.stem:
The grouped frequency table shows the time, in minutes, taken by 20 runners. Estimate the mean time.

| Time ($t$) | Frequency |
|---|---|
| $0 \le t < 10$ | 4 |
| $10 \le t < 20$ | 8 |
| $20 \le t < 30$ | 6 |
| $30 \le t < 40$ | 2 |
questions.explanation: Midpoints are 5, 15, 25 and 35. $\sum f \times m = 4(5) + 8(15) + 6(25) + 2(35) = 20 + 120 + 150 + 70 = 360$. Estimated mean $= 360 \div 20 = 18$ minutes.

questions.stem: For the ordered data set $5, 8, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 28, 31, 35$, what is the interquartile range?
questions.explanation: The lower half is $5, 8, 12, 15, 18$, so $Q_1 = 12$. The upper half is $21, 24, 28, 31, 35$, so $Q_3 = 28$. The interquartile range is $Q_3 - Q_1 = 28 - 12 = 16$.

questions.stem: In a survey of 60 people, 18 chose tea as their favourite drink. What angle would represent tea on a pie chart?
A survey of 40 students recorded how they travel to school. The table shows 22 walk and 18 cycle. What is the probability that a randomly chosen student cycles?
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{18}{40}$ students cycle. Simplifying by dividing numerator and denominator by 2 gives $\dfrac{9}{20}$.

questions.stem: A biased die has $P(6) = 0.35$. How many sixes would you expect in 150 rolls?
questions.explanation: Expected frequency $= P(\text{event}) \times \text{number of trials} = 0.35 \times 150 = 52.5$, which rounds to about 52 sixes.

questions.stem: The probability that a team wins a match is $0.65$. What is the probability that the team does not win?
questions.explanation: Using the complement rule: $P(\text{not win}) = 1 - P(\text{win}) = 1 - 0.65 = 0.35$.

questions.stem: The probability of rain on any day is $0.4$. Assuming days are independent, what is the probability it rains on Monday and Tuesday?
questions.explanation: For independent events, multiply the probabilities: $0.4 \times 0.4 = 0.16$.

questions.stem: A bar chart shows monthly sales for two shops. The vertical axis starts at $4000$ instead of $0$. Shop X has sales of $4200$ and Shop Y has sales of $4500$. Why is this graph misleading?
choices: The vertical axis does not start at zero, so the difference looks larger than it is.
questions.explanation: Starting the vertical axis above zero exaggerates the difference between bar heights. Here the actual difference is only $300$, but the bars may appear several times taller.

questions.stem: A scatter graph shows the outside temperature and the number of ice creams sold at a café. The points slope upwards from left to right. What does this show?
choices: Temperature causes people to buy ice cream.
questions.explanation: An upward trend means that as temperature increases, ice cream sales tend to increase too. This is a positive correlation. It does not prove causation on its own.

questions.stem: Two shops sell the same type of phone. Over a month, Shop A has a mean daily profit of $420 and a range of $380. Shop B has a mean daily profit of $410 and a range of $60. Which statement is true?
choices: Shop A has a higher average profit and more consistent profits.
Shop B has a lower average profit and more consistent profits.
Shop A and Shop B have the same average profit.
The range tells us the most common daily profit.
questions.explanation: Shop B's mean is lower ($410 < $420), but its range is much smaller ($60 < $380), so Shop B's daily profits are more consistent. The range measures spread, not the most common value.
